name: Algonquian Family

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Languages in this family utilize an animacy distinction (animate vs inanimate noun classes) rather than grammatical gender. Verbs, demonstratives, and quantifiers agree with the animacy class of their head noun. Animacy classification is partially arbitrary — some objects (e.g., raspberries, pants) are grammatically animate.

formality.description: Algonquian languages express formality through kinship-based respectful address and ceremonial language rather than pronominal T-V systems. Elder address and ceremonial contexts use specific vocabulary and discourse patterns.

linguisticChallenges.polysynthesis: Algonquian languages are highly polysynthetic. Verbs carry person markers for both subject and object, plus tense, aspect, mode, and derivational morphemes. A single verb form can express what requires a full clause in English.
linguisticChallenges.animacySystem: The animate/inanimate noun classification triggers agreement throughout the sentence — verbs, demonstratives, and quantifiers all agree with noun animacy. This system has no parallel in European languages.
linguisticChallenges.obviation: Algonquian languages have a proximate/obviative distinction for third-person referents — when two third-person entities interact, one is marked as 'proximate' (topical) and the other as 'obviative' (non-topical). This discourse-tracking system is typologically rare.
linguisticChallenges.directInverse: The direct/inverse voice system marks whether the subject or object is higher on the person/animacy hierarchy, replacing the active/passive distinction found in European languages.

contactInfluences.notes: English-only schooling policies (residential/boarding schools) severely disrupted intergenerational transmission across all Algonquian languages.
Fur trade era borrowings and missionary contact. French influence strongest in eastern Algonquian languages (Cree, Algonquin, Ojibwe).

notes: Family template for Algonquian languages (Cree, Ojibwe, Blackfoot, Mi'kmaq, etc.). All share polysynthetic morphology, animacy-based noun classification, obviation, and the direct/inverse voice system.
